name: Social contract
summary: Social contract theory holds that the legitimacy of political authority, and persons' moral and political obligations, rest on an agreement among the people who form a society, actual, tacit or hypothetical. It runs from Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau and Kant to the twentieth-century revivals of Rawls and Gauthier.
scope: The sources (IEP, SEP, Britannica) define social contract theory as the view that moral and/or political obligations depend on a contract or agreement among persons to form the society they live in. This profile covers the classical modern tradition (Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau, with Kant) and its contemporary contractarian (Gauthier: agreement among self-interested bargainers) and contractualist (Rawls: agreement among free and equal persons) revivals. Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau, Kant and Rawls are named by the sources as its thinkers, but are listed as key figures of other ideologies here, so their texts are tied through the key works. It takes the theory's own texts and the scholarship defining it. It excludes the feminist and race-conscious critiques (Pateman, Mills), which are critics of the theory, and the wider ideologies the individual thinkers belong to (absolutism, liberalism, republicanism), which hold more than the contract idea.

consent-of-governed.rationale: The core claim: political authority rests on agreement. Locke, Second Treatise §95: no one can be subjected to another's political power 'without his own consent'. Rousseau, Social Contract I.4: with no natural authority, 'the basis of all lawful authority is laid in mutual convention'. Hobbes's sovereign is likewise instituted by covenant (Gauthier, The Logic of Leviathan, the account of authorization). SEP: the traditional views of Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau 'crucially relied on the idea of consent'.

death-penalty.rationale: Execution of grave criminals is accepted by the main key works. Rousseau, Social Contract II.5: a malefactor 'becomes a rebel and traitor', and 'when a criminal is executed' he suffers as an enemy, not as a citizen; Locke, Second Treatise §7-§11: the right to punish crime, even by death, passes to the magistrate; Gauthier's The Logic of Leviathan discusses the sovereign's right to punish. Rousseau adds that executions signal weak government. Rawls's sources here are silent on it.
